recent_works.title: Ignition delay time of n-heptane under strained flow field in a counterflow configuration
recent_works.abstract: The overall ignition behaviors of n-heptane/nitrogen opposed by oxygen/ozone streams are experimentally observed, by measuring cool flame ignition (CFI) and hot flame ignition (HFI) delay times in a counterflow configuration. In agreement with the measurements, numerical simulations of the ignition process and the evolution of the maximum temperature show that higher strain rates lead to longer HFI delay times. A sensitivity analysis shows that strain rate plays stronger inhibitive impact on HFI delay than diffusivities of major species. On the contrary, strain rate promotes the transition from cool to hot flame behavior, whereas species diffusivities are insensitive to the transition time interval. Flame structures before and after CFI are analyzed along with species flux to explain the impact of strain rate on ignition behaviors. It is found that decomposition of ozone (O 3 → O 2 + O) accelerates the ignition of a cool flame, while R + O 2 → RO 2 reactions accelerate CFI-to-HFI transition. recent_works.title: Experimental Observation of Ammonia Blending and Cracking on Lean Blow-Out Behaviors in a Model Gas Turbine Combustor
recent_works.venue: Journal of Engineering for Gas Turbines and Power
recent_works.abstract: Abstract Ammonia is gaining attention as a carbon-free fuel for internal combustion engines in the context of global decarbonization efforts. However, its low reactivity poses challenges for stable combustion. This study investigates two strategies to enhance ammonia combustion: blending it with hydrocarbon fuels (methane) and partially cracking it to produce a hydrogen/nitrogen mixture. A model gas turbine combustor with optical access has been developed to investigate lean blow-out (LBO) behaviors. Experimental results show significantly different LBO behaviors between pure methane and ammonia, a factor of seven difference in global equivalence ratio. Ammonia blending with methane renders an increase of effective flame volume, thus suppressing overall reactivity, consequently resulting in the increased global equivalence ratio at LBO. Similar LBO behaviors are observed for ammonia cracking simulated by blending ammonia with hydrogen/nitrogen mixture, exhibiting hindered operability by reducing ammonia cracking fraction. recent_works.title: Effect of Exhaust Gas Recirculation on Combustion Efficiency in a Swirl Stabilized Flame With Blends of Natural Gas and Hydrogen
recent_works.venue: Journal of Engineering for Gas Turbines and Power
recent_works.abstract: Abstract Reducing the carbon impact of power-generation and industrial gas turbines can be achieved through blending of low-carbon fuels as well as carbon capture. In gas turbines, carbon capture is facilitated by the use of exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), where exhaust gases are mixed with inlet gases to increase carbon dioxide concentrations in the exhaust, which in turn increases the efficiency of carbon capture technologies. However, increasing the diluent fraction of the reactants can decrease flame static stability and lead to flame elongation, potentially affecting combustion efficiency and emissions. In this study, we measure emissions in a single-nozzle model combustor at a range of EGR levels and compositions for blends of natural gas (NG) and hydrogen (H2) to understand the impact of EGR on combustion efficiency. Different blends of diluents that mimic the effects of EGR are tested with oxygen mole fractions from 21% (no diluent injection) down to 15%. Blends of NG and H2 are tested with up to 40% H2 by volume. Flame imaging is used to better understand the connection between EGR, fuel composition, flame stabilization, and combustion efficiency. recent_works.title: Experimental Observation of Ammonia Blending and Cracking on Lean Blow-Out Behaviors in a Model Gas Turbine Combustor
recent_works.abstract: Abstract With a large focus on decarbonization in recent years, the use of ammonia has been proposed as a possible carbon-free fuel for internal combustion engines. The use of ammonia presents technical challenges, since ammonia exhibits considerably low reactivity compared to hydrocarbon fuels, including slow laminar flame speed, low energy density, and significantly narrow flammability. To cope with low reactivity of ammonia combustion, two approaches have been explored; blending with hydrocarbon fuel and/or integrating with ammonia catalysis cracker that converts ammonia to hydrogen/nitrogen mixture. The objectives of this study are to investigate the impacts of ammonia blending on hydrocarbon fuel and to evaluate the required ammonia cracking fraction on the operability of gas turbine combustors. A model gas turbine combustor with optical access has been developed, where the operability limit, lean blow-out (LBO) behaviors, can be experimentally determined by controlling fuel mass flow rate at various air mass flow rates at 1 atm at a maximum of 10 kW of thermal power.
